text:
Two points I grant, as my opening did: a passed test does not prove safety, and a brake written by the party that loses most from braking is weak.

But hidden capabilities do not spare a ban. To stop "short of the danger zone", someone must know where that zone begins. A model that can fool its testers can fool a treaty's inspectors too. Even a compute cap is set by asking what a given scale can do: an evaluation. Every ban needs a measured line, and that line is a tripwire.

Their burden of proof already fits this design. Anthropic's policy requires stronger safeguards not only when a threshold is crossed but whenever the company has not shown a model is well below it. That ambiguity triggered the Claude Opus 4 safeguards. A line that "holds when a test is ambiguous" is an if-then rule with a cautious default.

Who holds the pen is a fair worry about voluntary commitments, not about tripwires. Karnofsky ties their success to external auditors and regulation. Lab-run tests are funded; independent testers and binding law are what is missing. A treaty that never arrives moves no decision out of any lab.

sources.title: Activating AI Safety Level 3 protections (Anthropic, May 2025)
sources.quote: if models reach those thresholds (or if we have not yet determined that they are sufficiently far below them), we are required to implement a higher level of AI Safety Level Standards

sources.title: If-Then Commitments for AI Risk Reduction (Karnofsky, Carnegie Endowment, 2024)
sources.quote: the success of if-then commitments will likely depend on whether an ecosystem of qualified external auditors emerges, and on whether if-then commitments become backed by regulations (not just voluntary commitments)
